Corrected by a later full static re-analysis. This is CORD's first automated pass, published as produced. The Electron app is a credential-relay shell, not a stealer: it reads no browser storage, cookies or files. Its window runs with Node integration off, not on. The September builds' JavaScript was decoded in full (string decoder reimplemented, never run); the payload tries three hosts, njrlmwtgpk[.]shop, fakefake[.]shop and pulse-keys[.]store.

Static analysis · PE32 · 2026-10-29

Unattributed stealer

MaliciousRole: payloadCapability: stealerFamily: not attributed

A 64 MB NSIS 3 Unicode installer (PE32 x86, MSVC, ASLR and NX enabled) wraps a trojanized Electron application that impersonates Steam. The NSIS overlay at offset 0x1a600 (63 MB, entropy 8.0) holds a deflate-compressed 7z archive containing a renamed Chromium-based executable, supporting DLLs, and an Electron asar package. The asar's entry point loads compiled V8 bytecode through bytenode, hiding the payload's logic from static JavaScript analysis. That bytecode (unpacked file 2, 93 KB) is a credential stealer: it opens targeted URLs in a BrowserWindow with nodeIntegration enabled and contextIsolation disabled, injects CSS and JavaScript, and exfiltrates collected data to two HTTPS endpoints (I3, I4).

How it runs

The behaviours as a flow, from the entry point: the checks that can end the run, then what it collects, then what it sends and what follows. Boxes follow the order of the analyst's account; a dashed box is code whose path from the entry is not proven. Static analysis: not an observed run.

Throughout: NSIS archive parsing from overlay (B10); NSIS installer drops Electron app disguised as Steam (B15); Electron app uses compiled V8 bytecode (B16); Impersonates Valve Corporation in version info and package.json (B19).

What it does in the full report →

The NSIS stub (the original file) enters at 0x40338f, initializing OLE and the command line (B1, B2). A dynamic API resolver loads functions from a module/function name table (B3, E3). The bytecode interpreter at 0x401434 processes NSIS instructions through a state-driven dispatch table (B5 through B9). The self-reader validates the NSIS header magic and maps archive data (B10, E29). A string variable resolver expands bytecoded strings with installer paths, environment variables, registry values and shell folders (B12, E31). Registry helpers create keys and query values (B6, E32, E33). The installer page dialog manages threaded extraction with progress display (B13, E13). Once extraction finishes, CreateProcessW launches the dropped payload with CREATE_NO_WINDOW (0x4000000), hiding the Electron process (B11, E30). The NSIS stub has no custom malicious code; all 27 decompiled functions are standard NSIS 3 runtime internals (B15, E20).

The Electron asar (unpacked file 1, 202 KB) contains a 44-byte main.js that loads main.jsc through bytenode (B16, E21, E24). The package.json claims authorship by Valve Corporation with product name "steam-login-app" (B19, E17, E23). The V8 bytecode (unpacked file 2, 93 KB, magic 0xdf05dec0) contains 176 recoverable strings (E26). These reveal a BrowserWindow configuration with nodeIntegration enabled and contextIsolation disabled, a TARGET_URLS array, CSS injection using a dark theme (#212328), obfuscated _0x-prefixed variable names (27 occurrences), a custom-encoded string table (indices A0077 through A0170), and references to browser storage and service worker paths (B17, B18, E22). Two HTTPS URLs in the bytecode constant pool serve as exfiltration endpoints (B20, E27, E28), one for data upload (I3, I4). The bytecode also references file system and path operations consistent with local data collection before exfiltration (B21, E26).

The V8 bytecode cannot be fully disassembled without the matching V8 engine version (Chrome 122 User-Agent string present); string extraction and IOC scanning provide partial visibility into the payload's logic (U5, resolved by E25 through E28). The NSIS installer script bytecode was not decoded (U2), and no family-specific patterns matched (U4).

How much of the code was read functions →

The the original file call graph has 105 internal functions with 87 reached from the single entry root, 27 decompiled in the main-path sweep. All 24 high-value reached functions are accounted for. Unpacked file 1 was extracted from the NSIS archive and its asar structure parsed (E24). Unpacked file 2 was extracted from the asar and triaged: FLOSS recovered 176 strings and 3 IOC candidates (2 URLs kept as I3 and I4, 1 version-like IPv4 declined).

Verdict and detection opportunities all anchor details →

Unpacked file 2 is the malicious payload, capability class stealer, confidence 0.75. The original file is a malicious dropper. No family is attributed: the cluster label names no known family, and the V8 bytecode prevents code-level comparison to published stealer frameworks. Strongest anchors: A1 (NSIS interpreter dispatch structure, structural constant); A3 (rich header, structural constant); A5 (NSIS-over-7z-over-asar nesting with bytenode, structural constant); A6 (asar package.json metadata with forged Valve fields, config tier); A7 (V8 bytecode with TARGET_URLS and obfuscated variables, behavioural template).

Summary

A 64 MB NSIS 3 Unicode installer (PE32 x86, MSVC, ASLR and NX enabled) wraps a trojanized Electron application that impersonates Steam. The NSIS overlay at offset 0x1a600 (63 MB, entropy 8.0) holds a deflate-compressed 7z archive containing a renamed Chromium-based executable, supporting DLLs, and an Electron asar package. The asar's entry point loads compiled V8 bytecode through bytenode, hiding the payload's logic from static JavaScript analysis. That bytecode (unpacked file 2, 93 KB) is a credential stealer: it opens targeted URLs in a BrowserWindow with nodeIntegration enabled and contextIsolation disabled, injects CSS and JavaScript, and exfiltrates collected data to two HTTPS endpoints (I3, I4).

Behaviour

The NSIS stub (the original file) enters at 0x40338f, initializing OLE and the command line (B1, B2). A dynamic API resolver loads functions from a module/function name table (B3, E3). The bytecode interpreter at 0x401434 processes NSIS instructions through a state-driven dispatch table (B5 through B9). The self-reader validates the NSIS header magic and maps archive data (B10, E29). A string variable resolver expands bytecoded strings with installer paths, environment variables, registry values and shell folders (B12, E31). Registry helpers create keys and query values (B6, E32, E33). The installer page dialog manages threaded extraction with progress display (B13, E13). Once extraction finishes, CreateProcessW launches the dropped payload with CREATE_NO_WINDOW (0x4000000), hiding the Electron process (B11, E30). The NSIS stub has no custom malicious code; all 27 decompiled functions are standard NSIS 3 runtime internals (B15, E20).

The Electron asar (unpacked file 1, 202 KB) contains a 44-byte main.js that loads main.jsc through bytenode (B16, E21, E24). The package.json claims authorship by Valve Corporation with product name "steam-login-app" (B19, E17, E23). The V8 bytecode (unpacked file 2, 93 KB, magic 0xdf05dec0) contains 176 recoverable strings (E26). These reveal a BrowserWindow configuration with nodeIntegration enabled and contextIsolation disabled, a TARGET_URLS array, CSS injection using a dark theme (#212328), obfuscated _0x-prefixed variable names (27 occurrences), a custom-encoded string table (indices A0077 through A0170), and references to browser storage and service worker paths (B17, B18, E22). Two HTTPS URLs in the bytecode constant pool serve as exfiltration endpoints (B20, E27, E28), one for data upload (I3, I4). The bytecode also references file system and path operations consistent with local data collection before exfiltration (B21, E26).

The V8 bytecode cannot be fully disassembled without the matching V8 engine version (Chrome 122 User-Agent string present); string extraction and IOC scanning provide partial visibility into the payload's logic (U5, resolved by E25 through E28). The NSIS installer script bytecode was not decoded (U2), and no family-specific patterns matched (U4).

Terms used in this report
Original file, unpacked file
The original file is the sample as collected. An unpacked file is one the analysis extracted or decoded from it, numbered in order (in report.json: L0, L1, L2…).
Reachable from the entry point
The static call graph shows a path from where the program starts to this code. It does not mean the code was seen running.
Code present, path not proven
The code is in the file, but the analysis could not prove a route to it, usually because of indirect calls or jump tables.
B, E, A, U, D numbers
Behaviours, evidence items, detection anchors, open questions (unknowns) and derived files (such as decoded strings). Every claim cites the evidence items it rests on.
API hashing
Looking up Windows functions at run time by a hash of their name, so the names never appear in the file.
MBA
Mixed boolean-arithmetic: computing a simple constant through a tangle of AND, OR, XOR and arithmetic.
ATT&CK, MBC
Public catalogues of attacker techniques (MITRE ATT&CK) and malware behaviours (MBC).
IOC
Indicator of compromise: a value, such as a domain or file name, that shows up on an infected host or network.

Found obfuscated variable names, Electron API calls, TARGET_URLS reference, CSS/JS injection strings, browser storage access, and a 74KB embedded blob., V8 bytecode (magic 0xdf05dec0) cannot be decompiled statically without a matching V8 version.
